influences/candlemas-lupercalia/sourceCu: February purification rites and the Lupercalia (15 February), and the Robigalia procession against crop blight (25 April)
influences/candlemas-lupercalia/christia: Candlemas (Presentation of Christ / Purification of Mary, 2 February) with candle procession, and the Major and Minor Rogations
influences/candlemas-lupercalia/evidence: Candlemas originated in fourth-century Jerusalem as the fortieth day after Christ's birth (Luke 2:22–38), which is not a pagan source. The claim that it replaced the Lupercalia has no direct evidence. Gelasius I suppressed the Lupercalia c.495, but the Roman feast of 2 February with its procession is attested only under Sergius I (687–701). However, Bede (De temporum ratione 12) explicitly says Christians turned February's pagan lustral processions into the candlelit procession of St Mary. The Roman Major Litany of 25 April falls on the date of the Robigalia and is widely regarded as a probable Christian replacement. That part is plausible.
influences/candlemas-lupercalia/popularC: Candlemas is the Lupercalia (or the Celtic Imbolc) in Christian dress, and Valentine's Day and Rogation processions are pagan rites renamed.
influences/candlemas-lupercalia/whatHist: Egeria (c.383) describes the 'fortieth day after Epiphany' (14 February) in Jerusalem. Justinian moved it to 2 February in Constantinople in 542 as the Hypapante or 'Meeting', and Rome adopted it with a procession under Sergius I. The feast is therefore biblical and Eastern in origin. Gelasius' letter against the senator Andromachus shows that the Lupercalia survived in Christian Rome until c.495, and that a pope attacked rather than baptised it. Bede is the main early witness for a deliberate substitution, interpreting the candlelit procession as a Christian purification in place of pagan February rites. For the Rogations, Mamertus of Vienne (c.470) instituted three days of penitential processions before Ascension after disasters. The separate Roman Major Litany on 25 April followed a route along the Via Flaminia comparable to the Robigalia procession on the same date, and many liturgists from Duchesne onwards accept a replacement. The supposed Imbolc–Brigid–Candlemas link rests mostly on modern speculation.
influences/candlemas-lupercalia/summary: Candlemas is a biblical feast from Jerusalem, not a renamed Lupercalia, though medieval writers like Bede saw its candle procession as replacing pagan February purifications. The Roman Major Rogation on 25 April probably did take the place of the Robigalia procession for the crops.
influences/candlemas-lupercalia/story:
Luke's Gospel tells how Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the Temple forty days after his birth, where Simeon hailed him as 'a light to lighten the Gentiles' (Luke 2:22–38). The pilgrim Egeria saw this 'fortieth day' kept 'with the greatest joy' in Jerusalem around 383. In Constantinople, Justinian fixed it on 2 February in 542, during a plague, and the Greeks called it Hypapante, the Meeting of the Lord with Simeon. Rome received it in the seventh century. The Liber Pontificalis records that Sergius I (687–701) ordered processions from St Hadrian's to St Mary Major on four Marian feasts, including this one.

Rome's own February had been a month of purification (februa). Its most famous rite, the Lupercalia on 15 February, saw young men run around the Palatine striking bystanders with goatskin thongs for fertility and cleansing. The rite survived Christianisation for a century. Around 495 Pope Gelasius I wrote a letter against the senator Andromachus and his supporters, who blamed misfortunes on its neglect. Gelasius mocked the custom and insisted Christians abandon it. There is no record that a Christian feast was put in its place, and the Lupercalia's date does not match Candlemas.

Bede saw a connection all the same. In The Reckoning of Time (725) he says February takes its name from the Roman purifications, and that 'the Christian religion has changed this custom of purification for the better'. He means the candlelit procession on the feast of the Purification of St Mary. Blessing candles, from which the English name Candlemas comes, is attested in Gaul and England from about the tenth century. Medieval and early-modern folklore gave the day weather lore, the ancestor of America's Groundhog Day. The claimed link with Imbolc and St Brigid (1 February) comes mostly from modern writers.

The Rogations show the case for substitution more clearly. Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, instituted three days of fasting processions before Ascension c.470 after earthquakes and fires (Sidonius Apollinaris, Letters 5.14). The Council of Orléans (511) extended them across Gaul. Rome had a separate Litania maior on 25 April, the same day as the Robigalia, when Romans processed out of the city to sacrifice a dog to Robigus to keep rust off the grain. The Christian litany also processed out and back across the Milvian Bridge to pray for the crops. Most scholars take this as a deliberate Christian replacement, consistent with Gregory the Great's later advice to transform rather than abolish.

Rogation 'beating the bounds' processions survived in English parishes after the Reformation, with Elizabethan injunctions retaining perambulation of boundaries. Puritans attacked them as superstitious, and the 1970 Roman calendar left Rogation days to bishops' conferences. Candlemas remains a major feast in Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican calendars, closing the forty days of the Christmas cycle.

influences/aristotle-scholasticism/sourc: Aristotle’s logic, metaphysics of substance and accident, four causes, physics and ethics, transmitted via Boethius, Syriac and Arabic translators and Averroes
influences/aristotle-scholasticism/chris: Scholastic method in the universities, Thomist theology, the language of transubstantiation, Byzantine dialectic and Protestant orthodoxy
influences/aristotle-scholasticism/evide: The translation history, the Paris bans of 1210–1277, Aquinas’s commentaries on Aristotle and Luther’s attack on Aristotle in 1517 are all fully documented.
influences/aristotle-scholasticism/popul: Medieval Catholic doctrine, such as transubstantiation, was invented by applying pagan Aristotelian physics to the faith, and scholastic theology replaced the Bible with Aristotle.
influences/aristotle-scholasticism/whatH: Aristotle’s logic was used from late antiquity, but his natural philosophy and metaphysics entered Latin theology only in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, after the core doctrines of Trinity and incarnation had been defined (325–681). Belief in Christ’s real presence in the eucharist is far older; the word transubstantiation appears in the twelfth century and was used by the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, before the full reception of Aristotle’s physics, and Aquinas then explained it using substance and accident, while noting that it breaks Aristotle’s own rules. Aristotle provided method and terminology; theologians rejected his eternity of the world and mortal individual soul. Church authorities resisted him at first.
influences/aristotle-scholasticism/summa: Aristotle came late to Christian theology compared with Plato, but from the thirteenth century his logic and metaphysics became the backbone of university theology. The influence on method and terminology is undisputed; the claim that core doctrines were derived from him is not.
influences/aristotle-scholasticism/story:
Early Christian writers knew Aristotle mainly as a logician, and some, like Tertullian, distrusted him as the source of the heretics’ clever arguments. But logic was part of the standard curriculum through Porphyry’s Introduction (Isagoge), and during the christological controversies of the fifth to seventh centuries theologians on all sides used Aristotelian terms such as nature, essence, individual and property. John of Damascus prefaced his Fount of Knowledge (c. 743) with a Dialectica based on Porphyry and Aristotle, and Byzantine scholars continued to comment on Aristotle. Syriac Christians, notably Sergius of Reshaina (d. 536) and the scholars of the Church of the East, translated Aristotle’s logic; their work underlay the Abbasid translation movement in Baghdad.

In the Latin West Boethius (c. 477–524) translated the Categories and On Interpretation c. 510–520 and planned to translate all of Plato and Aristotle before his execution. For six centuries this ‘old logic’ was almost all of Aristotle the West possessed. In the twelfth century translators such as James of Venice, and Gerard of Cremona working from Arabic in Toledo, made the Physics, Metaphysics, On the Soul and Ethics available, often with the commentaries of Avicenna and Averroes; William of Moerbeke produced careful Greek-based versions in the 1260s.

The new Aristotle alarmed church authorities. Teaching his natural philosophy was banned at Paris in 1210 and 1215; Pope Gregory IX in 1231 ordered the books expurgated rather than suppressed; and in 1277 Bishop Étienne Tempier condemned 219 propositions, many tied to Latin Averroism, such as the eternity of the world and a single intellect for all humanity. Yet by 1255 the Paris arts faculty prescribed nearly all of Aristotle. Albert the Great and Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) undertook a critical integration: Aquinas wrote commentaries on twelve Aristotelian works and used his categories throughout the Summa Theologiae, while insisting on creation, providence and personal immortality against him. Aquinas’s ‘five ways’ adapt Aristotle’s argument for an unmoved mover.

The Reformation began partly as a revolt against this synthesis. In his Disputation against Scholastic Theology (September 1517) Luther declared that ‘the whole Aristotle is to theology as darkness is to light’ (thesis 50). Yet Philip Melanchthon soon restored Aristotle to the Wittenberg curriculum, and seventeenth-century Lutheran and Reformed orthodoxy (Gerhard, Turretin) used scholastic method extensively. The Council of Trent (1551) affirmed that the eucharistic change is ‘most aptly’ called transubstantiation, and Pope Leo XIII’s encyclical Aeterni Patris (1879) made Thomas the model for Catholic philosophy.

Orthodox theologians have often criticised Western scholasticism as overly rationalistic, a theme in the fourteenth-century debate between Gregory Palamas and Barlaam of Calabria and in the twentieth-century neo-patristic movement, though Byzantium had its own Aristotelian tradition. Historians today stress that scholasticism was a method of disputation and harmonisation, not the replacement of Scripture by philosophy: its sources were the Bible and the Fathers, organised in works such as Peter Lombard’s Sentences.
